e.etymology: The English verb cherish, to hold dear, from Old French cherir and Latin carus, dear. It joined the word names in the US in the later 20th century.

assoc.t: Cherish, hit songs by The Association and Madonna

e.etymology: Coined by Stephenie Meyer for Bella and Edward's daughter in Breaking Dawn (2008), the fourth Twilight novel, by blending the names of the child's grandmothers, Renee and Esme.
namesakes: Renesmee Cullen (Bella and Edward's daughter in Twilight)

assoc.t: Bella and Edward's daughter in the Twilight saga

e.note: Instantly read as a Twilight reference; in the books the character's nickname is Nessie.

e.etymology: From Old French Gislebert, from Germanic gisil (pledge) and berht (bright, famous). The Normans brought it to England.
namesakes: Gilbert Blythe (Anne's rival and love in Anne of Green Gables)

assoc.t: Gilbert, Arizona, a large Phoenix suburb
Gilbert and Sullivan, Victorian comic opera duo
Gilbert Grape, Johnny Depp's role in the 1993 film

e.etymology: A modern American name in the style of Deon and Leon. Keon is also an Irish surname, from Mac Eoghain, son of Eoghan.
The Yiddish and Ashkenazi Hebrew form of David, from Hebrew Dawid, beloved. In the US it is used mainly in Orthodox Jewish communities.

e.meaning: Roman god of war; the red planet
e.etymology: The name of the Roman god of war and of the fourth planet, named for him. The month of March and the names Marcus and Martin come from the same source.

assoc.t: Mars, the red planet
Mars, the Roman god of war
Mars, the candy maker behind M&M's and Snickers
pop star Bruno Mars
Mars bar, the chocolate candy bar

e.etymology: From Aramaic tabitha, gazelle. In the Book of Acts, Tabitha, called Dorcas in Greek, is a charitable woman of Joppa whom Peter raises from the dead.
namesakes: Tabitha Brown (actress and vegan food personality)

assoc.t: Tabitha, the young witch daughter on Bewitched

e.meaning: uncertain; read as lion of God or light of God
e.etymology: A biblical Hebrew name: Areli is a son of Gad (Genesis 46:16). Its meaning is uncertain; it is often tied to Ariel, lion of God, and older Bible dictionaries give light or vision of God. In the US it is mostly a Hispanic girl's name.
From Old Irish Cormac, earlier Corbmac: mac, son, plus corb, an obscure word glossed as chariot. Cormac mac Airt was a legendary high king of Ireland.
namesakes: Cormac McCarthy (novelist of The Road and Blood Meridian)

e.etymology: A 20th-century American coinage from Kay plus -lynn, a doubled-n spelling of Kaylyn. It also echoes Kayla and Caitlin.

e.meaning: gentle horse; later read as pretty rose
e.etymology: From Germanic hros (horse) and lind (soft, tender), reread in the Middle Ages as rosa linda, pretty rose. Shakespeare made it famous with the heroine of As You Like It.
namesakes: Rosalind Franklin (scientist whose X-ray work revealed the structure of DNA)
Rosalind (heroine of Shakespeare's As You Like It)

assoc.t: Rosalind, heroine of Shakespeare's As You Like It

e.meaning: Celtic name later tied to French triste, sad
e.etymology: A spelling of Tristan, from the Celtic name Drustan, reshaped by French triste, sad. Tristan is the knight of the medieval romance Tristan and Iseult.
A common Roman first name, probably from Latin lux, light. It was borne by three popes and passed into English use after the Renaissance.
namesakes: Lucius Malfoy (Draco's father in Harry Potter)
Lucius Fox (Batman's gadget maker, played by Morgan Freeman)

assoc.t: Lucius Malfoy, Death Eater in Harry Potter

e.etymology: A pet form of the Yiddish name Faiga or Feige, traditionally explained as bird, from Yiddish foygl, and paired with Hebrew Tzipporah. Used mainly in Hasidic and other Orthodox Jewish communities.
A modern Hebrew name, the feminine of Elior: Eli, my God, plus or, light.
From the Latin name Carinus, built on carus, dear, and borne by a 4th-century martyr. In northern Europe it also grew out of Karin, a form of Catherine. Carina is Latin for a ship's keel.

assoc.t: Carina, southern constellation with a famous nebula

e.meaning: Germanic name ending in frid, peace
e.etymology: A spelling of Jeffrey, the medieval English form of Geoffrey, a Norman name from Germanic. Its second part is frid, peace; the first is disputed, perhaps district, stranger or pledge.
e.note: Sounds the same as Jeffrey, borne by two infamous men, Jeffrey Dahmer and Jeffrey Epstein.

e.etymology: A respelling of Micah, from Hebrew Mikha, a short form of Mikhayahu, who is like Yahweh? Micah is one of the twelve minor prophets of the Hebrew Bible.
A pet form of the Yiddish name Gittel or Gitta, from Yiddish gut or git, good. Used mainly in Hasidic and other Orthodox Jewish communities.
The spelling of Victor used in German, Hungarian and the Scandinavian and Slavic languages, from Latin victor, conqueror. An early Christian favorite, borne by popes and martyrs.
namesakes: Viktor Frankl (psychiatrist, author of Man's Search for Meaning)
Viktor Krum (Quidditch star in Harry Potter)

assoc.t: Viktor, the inventor in Arcane and League of Legends

e.etymology: From Arabic sana, radiance or brilliance; in South Asia it is also read as Arabic thana, praise. Sana is separately a Japanese girl's name written with various kanji.

assoc.t: Sanaa, capital of Yemen, also spelled Sana

e.etymology: An Indian name from Sanskrit, glossed as inexhaustible or limitless. It sounds like Anya, the Russian pet form of Anna, but the two are unrelated.
A variant of Dion, a short form of Dionysius, the Greek name for a follower of Dionysus, god of wine. Deon is also the usual Afrikaans spelling in South Africa.

assoc.t: sounds like Deion, as in NFL star Deion Sanders

e.etymology: A respelling of Eliana, from Hebrew Eli (my God) and anah (answered). Eliana is also the Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of the Roman name Aeliana.
A K- spelling of Capri, the island in the Bay of Naples, in use as an American given name since the late 20th century.

assoc.t: sounds like Capri, Italian island in the Bay of Naples
sounds like capri pants, the cropped trousers
sounds like Capri Sun, the juice pouch drink

e.etymology: In Arabic, liyana means softness or gentleness, and the name is popular in Malaysia. It is also a spelling of Liana, a short form of Juliana and Liliana.

e.meaning: form of Katherine, long linked to Greek katharos, pure
e.etymology: The Norwegian form of Katherine, taken up in the US in the mid-20th century, where it also works as a spelling of Carrie. In Finland Kari is a man's name, from Macarius.
namesakes: Kari Lake (Arizona politician and former news anchor)

e.meaning: son of Madoc, a Welsh name meaning fortunate
e.etymology: A variant of the surname Maddox, son of Madoc, from the Welsh name Madog, built on mad, fortunate or good. Baseball fans know it from Hall of Fame pitcher Greg Maddux.

assoc.t: Greg Maddux, Hall of Fame pitcher
a Maddux, a shutout thrown in under 100 pitches

e.etymology: A modern name modeled on Hawaiian names such as Kalani, the heavens, and Keilani. Its rise follows the R&B singer Kehlani, whose name sounds the same.

assoc.t: sounds like Kehlani, the R&B singer

e.meaning: short form of Maria; also a Japanese name
e.etymology: A short form of Maria in Finnish, Estonian, Norwegian, Welsh and Spanish use, going back to Hebrew Miryam. Mari is also a separate Japanese girl's name written with various kanji.
From Persian and Arabic taj, crown, the word in Taj Mahal, crown of the palace. Used in South Asia and the Arab world and, since the later 20th century, in the US.

assoc.t: Taj Mahal, the marble mausoleum in Agra, India

e.etymology: A spelling of Coby or Kobe. In Hebrew, Kobi is the everyday short form of Yaakov, Jacob, traditionally glossed as supplanter. American use also echoes Kobe Bryant.

assoc.t: sounds like Kobe, as in Lakers legend Kobe Bryant
